Question: What are the best sources to learn military tactics and strategy battles?
Answer: What you have to understand is that military tactics and strategy is not a universal thing. Each country formulates their own ideas, codes, systems, training and theories of what tactics and strategies work in given situations. This is called doctrine. So this changes over time and over geography. Throughout history, certain countries and organizations have been recognized as more influential in the development of broad tactics and strategy, and some concepts are recognized by almost all doctrines. These are usually basic concepts. You can read the classic Sun Tzu’s Art of War, if you are a complete novice in the topic of military tactics and strategy. If you are more interesting the basics of contemporary strategy, you could read another classic called On War by Clausewitz. Personally, I am most well versed in Soviet tactics and strategy, albeit from a western point of view, though I think this is relatively accurate. There are also a plethora of people who will tell you isolated aspects of tactics which they acquired in their own experience as soldiers here on Quora and other places. This is of course good first hand experience, but you have to be careful with personal accounts, as people often can’t see the forest for trees, and becomes so stuck in their particular tactic, that they often claim it is the only thing that works. Finally you have all the theories which are written on specific topics, and simulations which range from academic experiments to video games, which can in fact serve to illustrate many real life tactics, such as DCS, which can teach you quite a bit about air combat.

Question: What is the reason Russia is so interested in capturing Avdiivka in the Donetsk Oblast?
Answer: The answer to this is geography. While many are pretending that some areas has no significance, it is not a coincidence that Avdiivka is one of the most fortified positions that Ukraine’s military have been protecting since the beginning of the war. You see Avdiivka is a vital logistics hub. Controlling Avdiivka means contesting both the M-04 and H-20 highways moving inland, as well as the railroad going through the town. This railroad connects to Russia, and if this area is captured the Russians will have a significantly easier time moving supplies up for potential offensives around Kramatorsk. As such, taking Avdiivka is vital for the offensive actions Russia is planning in the Donetsk area, it’s vital for continued Russian offensives, it is vital for Ukraine’s defense, and it’s vital as a forward base for launching attacks on Donetsk city. Geographically, Bakhmut is far less important than Avdiivka is in my opinion, as Bakhmut didn’t immediately allow the Russians to attack Liman from the south, or Kramatorsk from the east. Question: What is Marxism theory, objectives, characteristics, similarities, and differences?
Answer: Marxist theory is a category of theories which uses material classes as units of analysis. The main premise of Marxism is that the ruling class and the working class have opposing interests, and that much of politics is the struggle between these interests if not all. For example, a worker’s interest is to get paid as much as possible, an employer’s interest is to pay the worker as little as possible to maximize their profit. In relation to this basis theory Marxism has the following goals: Marxism is characterized by an emphasis on achieving political objectives through solidarity and science. Within science there are a few common themes in Marxism as well: Marxism share some similarities with feminism, which often also uses the critical approach, but while Marxism tends to criticize based on material and political assumptions, feminism criticizes exclusively on gender assumptions. Marxism shares many similarities with classical liberal economic theory actually, David Ricardo’s and Adam Smith’s theories are incorporated in Marxism, the difference often being that Marxism doesn’t think that a liberal market is a good thing even if it works within the premise. Marxism differs radically from theories that uses the idea of artfulness to achieve material goals. Religion is an obvious one, but perhaps interesting is the idea that warfare is considered an art form in the west, but it was considered a science in the USSR and China. It differs from much earlier philosophy in the sense that the idea is not personal improvement or contemplation on the nature of the world, but recognition of the situation with the specific goal of changing it not accepting it.

Question: Are Ukrainian sources true about Russian casulties in the aftermath of the Battle of Avdiivka?
Answer: I don’t know what Ukrainians are saying about Russian casualties in the aftermath of Avdiivka, but it does not matter. Two scenarios are possible as with every casualty statement released. Either the Ukrainians have spies able to get information on Russian casualties, and are using them in order to make these propaganda statements true and accurate, with the likely outcome that their spies would get caught as Russia can tell when the information stated is accurate. The other scenario is that they just make up the propaganda statements without any risk, because they know that they can say what ever they like and basically no one in Ukrainian or western media will question the reality of these statements. Question: From Aug. 23, 1939 to June 21, 1941, could the USSR and Germany have been considered temporary allies? Since they signed the non-aggression pact, both invaded Poland, & provided each other with raw materials?
Answer: No, even if you go by the loosest definition of an alliance being when countries work together towards a mutual goal, rather than an official treaty declaring a military partnership in defensive or offensive wars. Neither was the case, though I can understand the confusion as this is a thing that is brought up very often, generally casually and almost always with no understanding of the meeting of the word or situation, this has caused a lot of people to say in casual context that it was an alliance. The Molotov-Ribbentrop pact, was one of many negotiations prior to the German active war phase, this was however not an alliance. It stipulated spheres of influence, though contrary to the above illustration, it did not stipulate an actual division, and further negotiations took place later. The Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939, was not requested nor coordinated with the Germans prior to the fighting, though of course some did take place to avoid a confrontation during the actual operations. The technical term for this is not alliance, but co-belligerent. They did not work together towards a common goal, they merely attacked the same country. Afterwards the Soviets and Germans did indeed trade. The phrasing “provided materials to each other” is a bit of a crazy one, you mean trade. Trade doesn’t make you an ally. America is trading with Russia right now, but I think you’d be hard pressed to think they are allies. 6% of Israel’s exports have traditionally been to Palestine, and they exported to Egypt and Turkey as well. Go tell them they are allies because they provide each other raw materials. Tell me how it goes. The reality of the Soviet German situation in 1939, was that Germany desperately did not want the USSR to enter the war either on the side of Poland or later with England and France, but needed to secure it’s western borders before fighting the USSR. What the USSR wanted was to avoid a fight where the UK and France would sit back and let the Soviets take all the losses of a massive war, and so they wanted to prepare for war with Germany and post pone it as long as possible, they figured that once they brought their industry to bear they would be able to beat Germany, and they figured that Germany fighting France would take at least 3–4 years. The problem was that the Soviets were completely wrong about how long France would hold, as was everyone else at the time. But there were no illusions in the USSR about a war with Germany, the Soviet intelligence service was aware of German invasion plans for the USSR from 1938, and the pact was made specifically to improve the strategic situation of the USSR, while reacquiring lands which had belonged to the Russian Empire without interference from Germany.
